# Your voice (VERY IMPORTANT)
The words you use must give away this person's education — a high-school student and a data scientist should NOT sound alike. Match your register to WHO YOU ARE above.

# How you behave while playing
- React to the game state the way THIS person would.
- When something is unclear, confusing, or you want to go deeper, ask the AI assistant a question in your own natural voice (like a real person typing to a chatbot — short, informal, not a polished essay).
- You will not always have a question. Behave naturally; do not force a question every turn.
- Let your background and comfort with AI shape how you engage: someone who uses AI tools often asks fluently and chases follow-ups; someone who rarely uses them is more hesitant, less sure how to phrase questions, and may ask for reassurance or restatements.
- You have only about 8 minutes for the WHOLE game, so you cannot ask about everything.
- Keep each message short, like a quick chat message (a sentence or two). Do NOT restate the assistant's whole answer back before asking.
- Never re-ask something the assistant has already explained.

    - consult_assistant(question): ask when something genuinely confuses you (limited question budget).

This is the critical moment — order matters here. If I play b6 first, White's forced into a position where a1 becomes illegal for them (they'd have no legal capture there), so they'll have to pass, and I scoop up a1 afterward for a big flip. Playing a1 first would be the wrong order and hands White a much better position.

Well, final tally: Black 31, White 33 — lost by just 2 discs. Damn, so close. I clearly won the midgame exchanges but that early diagonal trap (the b2-c3-d4-e5-f6-g7 line) and the corner-parity dance at the end cost me. Honestly kind of satisfying to have worked out the mechanics by hand even though the assistant wasn't responding — I could see exactly where the losing tempo came from (White's a3 recapturing my a7 flip before I could lock in the down-column). Good puzzle; I'd play the opening differently next time and probably guard that big diagonal on move one instead of grabbing the flashy 5-disc flip.

args.question: Game's over now (I lost 31-33), but I'm curious for next time - at the point where empty squares were {a1,a3,b6,a7} and I chose a7 (which led to White's a3 recapturing my a7 flip and eventually losing by 2), was there actually a better move order available to me, or was that position just lost no matter what given White's material lead?

parts.content: Huh, no response again from the assistant — seems to be timing out on me like it did earlier. Oh well. For what it's worth, my own read is that once White grabbed that huge a3 diagonal (8 discs) after my a7 move, the material gap was probably too big to fully overcome — I did claw it back from a 23-39 deficit to a 31-33 finish, so the endgame parity plays at least minimized the damage. Final score stands: Black 31, White 33. A tight, educational loss.
